title: Sherlock Holmes and the Norwood Builder
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
retoldBy: Retold for Grammar Stream from “The Adventure of the Norwood Builder” by Arthur Conan Doyle (1903)
blurb: Cases for Young Detectives. A builder vanishes on the night he leaves his fortune to a young lawyer, and the police are sure the lawyer is to blame. Then a thumbprint appears on the wall, and Sherlock Holmes starts to laugh.
note: A retelling for young readers that keeps Doyle’s plot and Holmes’s deductions (the will written on a train, the thumbprint, the short corridor). In the original the police believe Oldacre has been murdered and burned; here they “fear the worst” and arrest McFarlane for an attack. The opening mention of Moriarty, the defaced photograph and the remains in the woodpile are left out. Nobody is hurt. “Clue check” questions are added.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. A Visitor in a Panic
paragraphs: “London has become a dull city for a detective,” said Sherlock Holmes one morning, pushing back his chair from the breakfast table. “Nothing interesting happens any more.”
He had hardly finished speaking when somebody began hammering on the front door. Feet clattered up the stairs, and a pale, untidy, wild-eyed young man burst into our room, gasping for breath.
“I’m sorry, Mr Holmes,” he cried. “You mustn’t blame me. I am nearly out of my mind. I am the unhappy John Hector McFarlane!”

“Do sit down, Mr McFarlane,” said Holmes calmly. “You speak as if I should know your name. But I assure you that, apart from the obvious facts that you are not married, that you are a lawyer, that you belong to the Freemasons and that you suffer from asthma, I know nothing whatever about you.”

I could follow my friend’s reasoning: the untidy clothes of a man with nobody to look after him, the legal papers in his pocket, the little badge on his watch-chain, and his wheezy breathing. But our visitor stared in amazement.
“Yes, I am all of those things, Mr Holmes. And I am also the unluckiest man in London. Please don’t turn me away! If the police come to arrest me before I have finished my story, make them wait.”
“Arrest you?” said Holmes. “What for?”
“They think I attacked Mr Jonas Oldacre, of Lower Norwood, and made him disappear!”
Our visitor picked up the newspaper from Holmes’s knee and pointed to the headlines. I read the report aloud.

It said that Mr Jonas Oldacre, a builder, lived alone with his housekeeper at Deep Dene House, in Lower Norwood. Late last night, a stack of wood in his timber-yard had caught fire and burned to ashes. Then people noticed that Mr Oldacre was missing. His bed had not been slept in. His safe stood open, with papers scattered all over the room. There were signs of a struggle, a few small spots of blood, and a walking stick with stains on its handle. Something heavy seemed to have been dragged from his window across the grass towards the woodpile. The police feared the worst.
And Mr Oldacre had had a late visitor in his room that night: a young lawyer from London called John Hector McFarlane. The walking stick belonged to him.
“I have been followed all the way here from the station,” said our visitor, wringing his hands. “It will break my mother’s heart!”
At that very moment there was a clang of the bell and heavy steps on the stairs. Our old friend Inspector Lestrade of Scotland Yard appeared in the doorway, with two policemen behind him.
“Mr John Hector McFarlane?” said Lestrade. “I arrest you for the attack on Mr Jonas Oldacre, of Lower Norwood.”
Poor McFarlane sank back into his chair as if he had been crushed.
“One moment, Lestrade,” said Holmes. “Half an hour can make no difference to you. This gentleman was just going to tell us his story.”
Lestrade looked at his watch. “Half an hour,” he said.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Strange Will
paragraphs: “Until yesterday, I hardly knew Mr Oldacre,” said McFarlane. “My parents knew him long ago, but they had not seen him for years. Then, yesterday afternoon, he walked into my office in London with some pages torn from a notebook, covered in scribbled writing.
“‘Here is my will,’ he said.” (A will, in case you don’t know, is a paper that says who will have your money and your house after you die.) “‘Please write it out properly for me, Mr McFarlane.’

“Imagine how astonished I was to find that he had left almost everything he owned to *me*! He was a strange, ferret-like little man with white eyelashes, and he was watching me with an amused look. He said he had no family, and that he had known my parents when he was young.

“Then he asked me to come to his house that very evening to look over his other papers. ‘And remember, my boy,’ he said, ‘not a word to your parents until everything is settled. We will keep it as a little surprise for them.’

“So I went to Norwood. His housekeeper let me in at half past nine. After supper, we went through the papers in his safe until nearly midnight. Then he let me out through the glass doors of his bedroom, which open into the garden. I couldn’t find my walking stick, but he said, ‘Never mind, my boy. I shall keep it until you come back.’ When I left him, he was alive and well, with the safe open and the papers in bundles on the table. It was too late to go home, so I slept at an inn nearby. I knew nothing more until I read the newspaper on the train this morning.”
“Anything you want to ask, Mr Holmes?” said Lestrade.
“Not until I have been to Blackheath,” said Holmes. Blackheath was where McFarlane’s parents lived.
“You mean to Norwood,” said Lestrade.
“Oh yes, I suppose that is what I must have meant,” said Holmes, with a little smile.
The policemen led McFarlane away. But Lestrade stayed, because Holmes was studying the scribbled pages of the will with great interest.
“There are some curious points about this, Lestrade,” said Holmes. “Look at the writing.”
“Well, the first few lines are clear,” said Lestrade. “And some in the middle, and some at the end. But the rest is very wobbly, and in three places I can’t read it at all.”

“It was written in a train,” said Holmes. “The good writing was done while the train stood at stations. The wobbly writing was done while it was moving, and the very bad writing while it rattled over the points, where the train changes from one track to another. So Mr Oldacre wrote his will on the train, on his way to see McFarlane. Isn’t it curious that a man should write something so important in such a careless way? It is almost as if he did not expect the will ever to matter.”

“Well, it is clear enough to me,” said Lestrade. “Here is a young man who suddenly finds out he will be rich if the old man disappears. He tells nobody. He goes to the house at night. When the housekeeper has gone to bed, he attacks the old man, tries to hide what he has done by burning the woodpile, and goes off to an inn.”

“It seems to me, my good Lestrade, a little *too* clear,” said Holmes. “If you were that young man, would you choose the very same night that the will was made? Would you go when a servant had let you in and knew you were there? And would you take great care to hide everything, and then leave your own walking stick behind? Confess, Lestrade, that it is very unlikely.”
“Criminals often panic and make silly mistakes,” said Lestrade. “Have you got a better idea?”

“I could give you half a dozen. Here is one. A passing tramp sees the old man through the window, with his valuable papers. When the young man has gone, the tramp climbs in, grabs the stick and attacks him.”
“Then why didn’t the tramp take anything?”
“Because they were papers he could not sell.”
Lestrade shook his head. “Well, the future will show which of us is right,” he said, and off he went.
Clue check: Mr Oldacre wrote his will in a hurry, on a bumpy train, and then made McFarlane promise not to tell his parents. Why might somebody write a will that he does not expect ever to matter?

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Everything Goes Wrong
paragraphs: “Why Blackheath first, Holmes?” I asked.

“Because there are two strange things in this case, Watson: first, a will made suddenly to a young man the old builder hardly knew; and second, a disappearance on the very same night. The police are only looking at the second thing. I want to understand the first.”
He set off alone. It was late when he came back, tired and worried. For an hour he scraped gloomily on his violin. At last he threw it down.
“It is all going wrong, Watson,” he said. “For once, I believe Lestrade may be right and I may be wrong. All my instincts point one way, and all the facts point the other.

“I went to Blackheath. Mrs McFarlane told me that she had known Jonas Oldacre well, long ago. In fact, he had wanted to marry her! But then she heard how cruel he had been to some animals, and she would have nothing more to do with him. She married a kinder man instead. Jonas Oldacre never forgave her.
“‘Well,’ I said, ‘at least he has forgiven you now, since he has left all his money to your son.’
“‘Neither my son nor I want anything from Jonas Oldacre!’ she cried.

“Then I went to Norwood. In the ashes of the woodpile, the police had found some burnt buttons from Mr Oldacre’s trousers. I crawled about the lawn for an hour, but the ground was baked as hard as iron. In the bedroom there were only the footprints of Oldacre and McFarlane. No tramp!
“I spoke to the housekeeper, Mrs Lexington, a small, dark, silent woman with sly, sideways eyes. She knows something, Watson, I am sure of it. But she would tell me nothing.

“There was one tiny gleam of hope. I looked through Mr Oldacre’s bank book. In the last year he had paid large sums of money to somebody called Mr Cornelius. Who is Mr Cornelius? I should very much like to know.”
The next morning, Holmes was pale and tired, as if he had not slept at all. A telegram lay on the table. It was from Lestrade:
IMPORTANT FRESH EVIDENCE. McFARLANE’S GUILT DEFINITELY PROVED. ADVISE YOU TO GIVE UP CASE.
“This sounds serious,” I said.
“It is Lestrade’s little cock-a-doodle-doo of victory,” said Holmes. “But fresh evidence can cut both ways. Come, Watson. I think I shall need your company today.”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Thumbprint on the Wall
paragraphs: At Deep Dene House, Lestrade met us at the gate, beaming with triumph.
“Well, Mr Holmes, have you found your tramp yet?” he said. “Step this way, gentlemen. I can prove once and for all that it was John McFarlane.”
He led us into a dark hall by the front door. “This is where McFarlane must have come to fetch his hat after the deed was done,” he said. “Now look at this!”
He struck a match. On the whitewashed wall, in the flickering light, was a small red mark. As he held the match closer, I saw that it was more than a mark. It was the print of a thumb.
“You know that no two people in the world have the same thumbprint?” said Lestrade.
“I have heard something of the kind,” said Holmes.
“Then compare it with this.” Lestrade held up a piece of wax. “This morning I made young McFarlane press his right thumb into it.”
I did not need a magnifying glass to see that the two prints were exactly the same. Our poor client was lost.
“That is final,” said Lestrade.
“Yes, that is final,” I echoed sadly.
“It is final,” said Holmes.
Something in his voice made me turn round. An extraordinary change had come over his face. His eyes were shining like stars. He seemed to be trying desperately not to burst out laughing.
“Dear me! Dear me!” he said at last. “Who would have thought it? And such a nice young man, too! It shows that we should not trust our own opinions, eh, Lestrade? By the way, who found this mark?”
“The housekeeper, Mrs Lexington. She showed it to the policeman on guard last night.”
“I suppose there is no doubt that the mark was there yesterday?”

Lestrade looked at Holmes as if he had gone mad. “I suppose you don’t think McFarlane broke out of prison in the middle of the night just to put more evidence against himself?” he said. “I am writing my report.” And he marched off.
“This is a sad development, Watson, is it not?” said Holmes. But his eyes were still twinkling. “And yet there is one really serious flaw in this evidence.”
“What is it, Holmes?”
“Only this. I *know* that mark was not there when I looked at this hall yesterday. And now, Watson, let us take a little stroll in the sunshine.”

My head was spinning, but my heart was full of hope again. Holmes walked all round the outside of the house, looking up at every wall. Then he went inside and climbed from the cellar right up to the attic, looking into every room. On the top floor, in a long, empty corridor, Holmes paced slowly from one end to the other, counting his steps under his breath. Then he began to shake with silent laughter.
“There are some really unusual things about this case, Watson,” he said. “I think it is time we let our friend Lestrade into the secret.”

Clue check: Holmes is sure the thumbprint was put on the wall during the night. But McFarlane was locked up in a police cell. So who could have put it there? And why did Holmes count his steps along the top corridor?

chapters.title: Chapter 5. “Fire!”
paragraphs: “I think your report is a little early, Lestrade,” said Holmes. “There is an important witness you have not seen yet.”
“Can you bring him here?”
“I think I can. How many policemen have you?”
“Three.”
“Excellent! Are they all big, strong men with loud voices?”
“I suppose so, though I can’t see what their voices have to do with it.”
“Perhaps I can help you to see that, and one or two other things as well,” said Holmes.

He asked the policemen to fetch two bundles of straw and two buckets of water, and led us all up to the long corridor on the top floor. The constables were grinning. Lestrade looked as if he could not decide whether to be curious or cross.
“Put the straw here on the floor, away from the walls,” said Holmes. “Now, Watson, would you open that window and light the edge of the straw?”
I did so, with the buckets of water standing ready beside me. Grey smoke began to swirl down the corridor, and the dry straw crackled.
“Now,” said Holmes, “I would like you all to shout ‘Fire!’ One, two, three—”
“FIRE!” we all yelled.
“Thank you. Once more, please.”
“FIRE!”
“Just once more, gentlemen, all together.”
“FIRE!” The shout must have rung right across Norwood.

It had hardly died away when an amazing thing happened. At the end of the corridor, a door suddenly flew open in what had looked like solid wall, and a little wrinkled man darted out of it, like a rabbit out of its burrow.
“Capital!” said Holmes calmly. “Watson, a bucket of water over the straw, please. That will do! Lestrade, allow me to present your missing witness: Mr Jonas Oldacre.”
Lestrade stared in blank amazement at the little man, who stood blinking in the light with his shifty pale-grey eyes and white eyelashes.
“What’s this?” cried Lestrade. “What have you been doing all this time, eh?”
Oldacre gave a nervous laugh. “I have done no harm,” he said. “It was only a joke.”
“A joke!” said Lestrade, going redder and redder. “You did your very best to get an innocent man locked up for the rest of his life! Take him downstairs!”

When the policemen had taken him away, Lestrade turned to Holmes. “Mr Holmes,” he said, “this is the brightest thing you have ever done, though it is a mystery to me how you did it. You have saved an innocent man.”

A thin wall had been built across the end of the corridor, with a cleverly hidden door. Behind it was a little room with a bed, food and water, and a pile of papers. “There’s the advantage of being a builder,” said Holmes. “He could make his own hiding place, with nobody to help him but his housekeeper.”
“But how did you know he was there?” asked Lestrade.

“When I paced along this corridor, I found it was six feet shorter than the one on the floor below. So there had to be a secret space at the end. I guessed he would not have the nerve to stay quietly hidden if he thought the house was on fire.”
“But how did you know he was in the house at all?”

“The thumbprint, Lestrade. You said it was final, and so it was, but not in the way you meant. I knew the mark was not on the wall the day before, so somebody must have put it there in the night. Here is how. When Oldacre and McFarlane were sealing up the bundles of papers with hot wax, Oldacre must have asked McFarlane to press his thumb on to one of the soft seals. It would be done so quickly and naturally that McFarlane probably does not even remember it. Then, hiding in his secret room, Oldacre had a wicked idea. He made a copy of the thumbprint from that seal, pricked his own finger for a drop of blood, and crept down in the night to press the mark on to the wall. I am sure you will find that seal among the papers in his hiding place.”
“Wonderful!” said Lestrade. “But why did he do all this?”

“Revenge, Lestrade, and money. Long ago, McFarlane’s mother refused to marry him, and he never forgave her. You would have known that if you had gone to Blackheath first. And lately Oldacre has been losing money and owes a great deal. So he has been quietly paying his money to ‘Mr Cornelius’, who I am sure is Oldacre himself under another name. He meant to vanish, start a new life as Mr Cornelius, and keep the money, and at the same time take his revenge by making it look as if her son had attacked him. The will, the secret visit, the stick, the stains, the old trousers burnt in the woodpile: it was a very clever plan. But he did not know when to stop. He tried to make it even more perfect with the thumbprint, and that is what gave him away.”
Lestrade shook Holmes warmly by the hand. “And you don’t want your name in the newspapers, Mr Holmes?”
“Not at all,” said Holmes, smiling. “The work is its own reward. Write your report, Lestrade, and let everybody see how hard it is to fool the police.”
That afternoon, John Hector McFarlane walked out of the police station a free man, and went home to his mother at Blackheath.
